r: Sleep loss harms memory at both ends of its pipeline. Matthew Walker's group found that one sleepless night cuts the hippocampus's capacity to encode new information by roughly 40%, much like an inbox nobody has emptied that can't take new mail. The deeper damage happens offline. During slow-wave sleep, 0.5–1 Hz oscillations occur alongside 11–16 Hz spindles and hippocampal sharp-wave ripples. Together they replay the day's memory traces and send them to the neocortex for long-term storage. If you skip that night shift, consolidation stalls. Researchers suspect the brain's glymphatic system, which clears waste, also falls behind. In mice, its interstitial channels widen by about 60% during sleep. Without that clearing, metabolic debris such as amyloid-beta may cloud the next day's learning. Even partial restriction adds up: subjects held to six hours of sleep for two weeks did as poorly on attention tests as people who were totally sleep-deprived, yet they rated themselves as only mildly impaired. In short, memory is built by day but stored at night.
